cloze.s: The senior partner's ___ manner with the new interns, offering gentle advice over coffee like a kindly family elder, put them at ease.

why: 'an ___' let only vowel-initial words fit; just 1 of 9 wrong options did, so the article gave the answer away
'sought the avuncular elder's advice' also makes sense in the cloze
'hidebound about protocol, insisting guests be seated by rank' also fits the cloze
'his uncle's prolix speeches' also fits the cloze
loud, unruly behavior overlaps; 'obstreperous young executive ... talked over anyone' also fits the cloze
fusty also means stale or musty smelling; 'the fusty smell' fits the cloze and overlaps the def

set.note: Named after Stentor, a Greek in Homer's Iliad whose voice was as loud as fifty men's.
set.story: In Homer's Iliad (Book 5), the goddess Hera takes the form of Stentor, a Greek with a voice of bronze who could shout as loudly as fifty other men.

why: The Iliad never calls Stentor a herald (Iliad 5.785-786 only describes his voice); 'herald' comes from later sources

cloze.s: The scientist argued that further sea-level rise was now ___: no policy could stop it entirely, only slow it.

why: 'an ___' made it a giveaway: none of the 9 wrong options starts with a vowel
'mean' in the sense of stingy is chiefly British; the spec requires American usage

cloze.s: Announcing layoffs on the same day as the executive bonuses was a deeply ___ move that angered the whole staff.

why: 'an ___' let only vowel-initial words fit; just 1 of 9 wrong options did, so the article gave the answer away
noisome also means harmful or noxious (its original sense), so it overlaps the def
'Many countries circumscribe the sale of ivory' (restrict it) also makes sense in the cloze
proscribe can also mean to outlaw or banish a person; it might be read as fitting the cloze

cloze.s: Priya's parents ___ her by showing her new boyfriend her baby photos from the bathtub.

why: Removed 'naked' from the cloze to keep it tasteful
chasten (to humble) is close to mortify (to humiliate), so it is too close to use as a wrong answer
'The failed launch mortified the overconfident founders' also fits, and humbling overlaps humiliating
fulminate also means to criticize severely (WordNet 'criticize severely'), so it overlaps the def
'housing and other perquisites that came with the post' fits the cloze, arguably better
emolument covers payments and benefits from an office, so it overlaps the def

ex: Years of sycophancy from his staff left the CEO unable to accept any criticism.
Wei's honest feedback was a refreshing change from the sycophancy of the other advisers.

why: 'surrounded himself with sycophancy' is unnatural; people surround themselves with sycophants

ex: The street vendors stayed in the plaza only on the sufferance of city officials.
After the argument, Olga felt she was at the family dinner only on sufferance.

why: 'on sufferance of the city' is unidiomatic; the idiom is 'on the sufferance of'
'nothing but financial dissimulation' (deception) could also fill the cloze
'the nurse's bonhomie never faded; she greeted every patient with a joke' fits the cloze, and the cheerful senses overlap
'seemed to go on indefatigably' (tirelessly, without stopping) could be read as fitting the cloze
peremptorily (WordNet 'in an imperative and commanding manner') and cavalierly (WordNet 'proud and domineering') overlap the def and could fit 'waved ___ at her servants'
'imperiously/cavalierly banned the band' also makes sense in the cloze, and imperiously overlaps the commanding sense
'peremptorily dismissed the breach' could also fit the cloze
